parrafos.texto: Let me tell you about thirteen seconds that changed music forever.
Las Vegas. September 7, 1996. Quarter past eleven at night.
A black BMW stops at a red light. Suge Knight is driving. Tupac Shakur sits beside him.
Now look to your right.
A white Cadillac pulls up. Slowly.
The back window comes down.
Tupac is hit four times. Six days later, he is dead.
But here's what nobody tells you. It started hours earlier… in a hotel lobby.
Part two.
Hours before that red light, Tupac was standing in a casino lobby.
MGM Grand, Las Vegas. Mike Tyson had just won a fight in under two minutes.
Then someone points at a young man. Orlando Anderson.
Tupac runs at him. His crew joins in.
Security cameras record every second.
Nobody presses charges. It looks like nothing.
But Anderson wasn't alone in Las Vegas that night. His uncle was in town too.
And according to the man in the front seat, that night, a white Cadillac went looking for Tupac.
Part three.
Here's the strange part. Dozens of people rode in Tupac's convoy. Almost nobody talked.
One friend, in the car right behind, refused to help police. Two months later, he was shot dead in an unrelated case.
Orlando Anderson was arrested. Then released. He denied everything.
Six months later, The Notorious B.I.G. was killed too. Another drive-by.
In 1998, Anderson himself was shot dead in Compton.
The case went cold.
But one man from that Cadillac was still alive. And he couldn't stop talking.
Part four.
Imagine admitting you were in the car… in the most famous murder in hip-hop. On television.
His name is Duane Davis. Keffe D. Orlando Anderson's uncle.
In 2008, he told detectives his story. In secret, under a deal that protected him.
Ten years later, he said it on camera. Front passenger seat. The shots came from the back.
Then he wrote a book about it.
That deal didn't cover any of it.
In September 2023, police arrested him.
Part five.
Twenty-nine years after that red light, a jury finally heard the story.
Las Vegas, August 2026. No gun. No fingerprints. No new witness.
Just his own words. Every interview. Every page of his book.
The defence called it street stories, told for money.
The jury needed less than three hours.
Guilty. Forty years to life. He says he'll appeal.
But one question never reached a courtroom. According to him, the shooter was his own nephew… who died in 1998.
The case is closed. The questions aren't.
